opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the big one is just economics and speed. Opus is our most capable model, and it's really good at the hard parts: understanding a messy codebase, figuring out what the actual plan should be, noticing when something doesn't add up. But a lot of the work in a real coding session isn't that. It's things like "go read these twenty files and tell me where this function gets called," or "run the test suite and summarize the failures," or "make this same mechanical change in fifteen places." You don't need your most expensive, most thoughtful model doing all of that serially.

So having Opus act more like a tech lead, where it breaks the problem down and hands well-scoped pieces to Sonnet subagents, gets you a few things at once. You get parallelism, so several of those pieces can be happening at the same time instead of one after another. You get lower cost per task, which matters a lot when people are running these agents for hours. And maybe less obviously, you get cleaner context. Each subagent starts with a focused window on just its piece, so it isn't dragging around a giant history of everything else that's happened, and the orchestrator only gets back the distilled result rather than all the noise from the search. That actually helps quality, not just cost, because long, cluttered contexts are where models start to lose the thread.

The other thing I find interesting is that it mirrors how good human teams work. Your senior engineer shouldn't be the one grepping through logs all day. They should be deciding what matters and reviewing the output. And as the smaller models keep getting better, the set of things you can safely delegate keeps growing, so the overall system gets more capable even faster than any single model does.

There are real tradeoffs. Delegation only works if the task is specified well, and if a subagent comes back with something subtly wrong, the orchestrator needs to catch it. So a lot of the work is in getting the model to write good task descriptions and to actually verify results instead of just trusting them. But when it works, it feels a lot less like using a tool and a lot more like managing a small team, and I think that's directionally where things are heading.

r001.rationale: It says Sonnet subagents can read files and trace function calls in parallel, so the searches happen at once rather than serially, improving speed.

r002.rationale: It says each subagent gets a focused context and Opus receives only a distilled result, limiting search-related context in the orchestrator.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that most real engineering work isn't one hard problem, it's one hard problem surrounded by a lot of pretty mechanical work. You need to figure out the right architecture or track down a subtle bug, and that's where you want the smartest model you have. But then there's a long tail of stuff like "go find every call site of this function," "run the test suite and tell me what broke," "read these twelve files and summarize what they do." Those tasks are important, but they don't need the frontier model thinking really hard about them.

So when Opus is acting as the orchestrator and farming that work out to Sonnet subagents, you get a few things. The obvious one is cost and latency. Sonnet is faster and cheaper, so you can run a bunch of these in parallel and the whole task finishes sooner than if one model did everything serially.

The less obvious benefit, and honestly the one I care more about, is context management. A big codebase is way larger than any context window, and even within the window, the more junk you stuff in there, the worse the model gets at the thing that actually matters. If Opus has to read every file itself, it's spending its attention on noise. When a subagent goes off, reads a thousand lines, and comes back with a two-paragraph summary, Opus gets to keep its context clean and focused on the decision it needs to make. It's a bit like how a good tech lead doesn't personally read every line of the codebase. They ask someone to go investigate and report back.

There's also a robustness angle. If a subagent goes down a rabbit hole or gets confused, that failure is contained. It doesn't pollute the main thread of reasoning. The orchestrator can look at the result, decide it doesn't trust it, and send someone else or do it itself.

I'll say the thing we're still learning is how to make the delegation good. Writing a crisp task description for a subagent is a skill, and models aren't perfect at it yet. Sometimes Opus under-specifies and the subagent comes back with the wrong thing, sometimes it over-delegates something it could have just done. But the direction is clearly right. As the models get better at knowing what they don't need to do themselves, you get this really natural division of labor that looks a lot like how a well-run team works.

r001.rationale: It says Sonnet is faster and cheaper, so searches can run in parallel and the task finishes sooner than doing everything serially.

r002.rationale: It explains that subagents read files and return summaries, keeping Opus’s context clean and focused.

astra-6.text:
The big benefit is a division of labor. Opus can keep track of the overall goal, reason through the harder architectural decisions, and break the work into pieces. Then Sonnet subagents can handle more bounded tasks—investigating a particular part of the codebase, implementing a change, or running tests—in parallel.

That can give you a better combination of capability, speed, and cost than having Opus do everything itself. It also helps manage context: each subagent can focus on its own task and bring back the relevant findings, rather than putting every intermediate detail into the main conversation.

The catch is that delegation has overhead. You need clear task boundaries, and Opus still needs to check that the pieces fit together. So I think it’s especially useful for larger tasks where there’s genuinely independent work to do.

r001.rationale: It says Sonnet subagents can investigate parts of the codebase in parallel and that delegation improves speed, communicating reduced latency for those searches.

r002.rationale: It says each subagent focuses separately and returns relevant findings instead of putting every intermediate detail in the main conversation, communicating reduced consumption of Opus’s context.

sol-6.1.text: The big benefit is that you can separate figuring out what needs to be done from doing every piece of it. Opus can hold the overall plan and delegate more bounded tasks to Sonnet—exploring part of the codebase, implementing a change, or checking something—and then bring the results back together. You get parallelism, potentially lower cost and latency, and you keep all the intermediate detail from filling up the main agent’s context. The challenge is making the tasks clear enough that the subagents can work independently, and making sure the coordinating agent actually checks how the pieces fit together.

r001.rationale: The response includes codebase exploration among the delegated tasks and says delegation enables parallelism and potentially lower latency.

r002.rationale: It says delegation keeps intermediate detail from filling the main agent’s context, covering the context cost of delegated codebase exploration.
